children.label: Overview
children: Seeing the patient before surgery to identify risks that may affect recovery
Visit done one day before surgery
Aim: lower anesthetic and surgical morbidity and mortality, patient in optimal condition
Steps: problem identification, risk assessment, preoperative preparation, plan of anesthetic technique
Technique options: GA, laryngeal mask, endotracheal tube, spinal, epidural, local

children.label: Purposes
children: Document the condition needing surgery
Define the patient's medical and surgical problems
Arrange investigations, consultation and treatment if not optimal
Develop the anesthetic technique and perioperative care plan
Inform and reassure the patient
Reduce cost, hospital stay and cancellations

children.label: History
children: Brief history of present illness, current medications, allergies and reaction type
Past medical and surgical history, past anesthetic history
Family history of anesthetic problems
Functional inquiry and NPO status
Special attention to CVS, respiratory and neuromuscular systems
Unstable symptoms: postpone elective surgery for optimization

children.label: Cardiovascular and respiratory points
children: MI within 6 months or unstable angina: poor surgical candidate
Ask about exercise tolerance, arrhythmia or pacemaker, hypertension
Valvular disease: consider risk of subacute bacterial endocarditis
Active cardiac conditions: postpone except life-saving emergencies
COPD: baseline CO2 is high (50-60), avoid aggressive hyperventilation
Asthma: airway manipulation and cold dry gases trigger attacks
Acute URTI: postpone elective surgery about 6 weeks
Sleep apnea: may need postoperative ventilatory support

children.label: Smoking cessation timeline
children: Advise stopping at least 8 weeks before surgery
12-24 h: CO and nicotine levels fall
48-72 h: COHb normalizes, airway function improves
1-2 weeks: less sputum
4-6 weeks: PFTs improve
6-8 weeks: immune function normalizes
8-12 weeks: lower overall postoperative morbidity

children.label: Other conditions
children: Epilepsy: optimize antiepileptic dosing, avoid enflurane
Spinal cord injury: respiratory failure, autonomic hyperreflexia, hyperkalemia
Myasthenia gravis and NMJ disorders: unpredictable response to NMBs
Muscular dystrophy: higher malignant hyperthermia risk and postoperative respiratory failure
Diabetes: delayed gastric emptying, silent MI, stop oral hypoglycemics and use insulin sliding scale
Goitre: airway compression and tracheal deviation, inhalational induction preferred
Hyperthyroid: thyroid storm risk; hypothyroid: myocardial depression
GERD: H2 blocker, citrate, cricoid pressure
Long-term steroids: stress-dose steroids to prevent Addisonian crisis

children.label: Medications and allergies
children: Take cardiac and pulmonary medications with sips of water up to the day of surgery
Ask about penicillin, latex and propofol (egg) allergy
Lecturer: egg allergy is to egg white while propofol contains yolk lecithin
Metformin: stop a few days before surgery
Beta blockers decrease cardiovascular mortality
Asthmatics: avoid histamine-releasing drugs (morphine, atracurium)

children.label: Malignant hyperthermia and scoline apnea
children: MH: familial, fatal, triggered by inhalational agents (except N2O) and succinylcholine
MH preparation: total IV anesthesia, vaporizer disconnected, room ventilated 6 h, first case of the day
Dantrolene: lecturer stressed it only eases symptoms (standard teaching: the specific MH treatment)
Scoline apnea: pseudocholinesterase deficiency, prolongs ventilation, less dangerous than MH
Prolonged apnea in family suggests pseudocholinesterase deficiency; unexplained death suggests MH

children.label: Fasting guidelines
children: 8 h: meat, fried or fatty meal
6 h: light meal, infant formula, non-human milk
4 h: breast milk
2 h: clear fluids
Emergency with short fast: signed high-risk consent, rapid sequence induction with suxamethonium

children.label: Four fatal things in anesthesia
children: Malignant hyperthermia
Anaphylaxis
Aspiration
Disconnection of the circuit

children.label: Airway assessment
children: TMJ mobility: one-finger groove at the tragus on mouth opening
Mouth opening: three fingers should fit
Thyromental distance: less than 7 cm suggests difficult intubation
Mallampati I-II easy, III-IV difficult
Also tracheal centralization, upper lip bite (Calder) test, cervical spine mobility, Wilson score
Down syndrome (large tongue) and micrognathia: difficult intubation
Cervical spine disease (e.g. RA): awake intubation without neck extension

children.label: Investigations
children: CBC for every patient, others guided by history and examination
ECG: age over 50, hypertension, IHD signs, arrhythmia, diabetes over 40
Chest X-ray: cardiac or respiratory disease, malignancy, thoracic surgery
U&E, LFT, blood sugar, coagulation screen, urinalysis by indication
PFTs for dyspnea, COPD or asthma; cervical spine X-ray if difficult intubation predicted
ABG if dyspneic or cyanosed at rest, FEV1 below 60%, or thoracic surgery

children.label: ASA physical status
children: I: healthy patient
II: mild systemic disease, no limitation (also smoker, pregnant, obese, over 80 y)
III: severe systemic disease with definite limitation (e.g. IHD, COPD, morbid obesity)
IV: severe disease that is a constant threat to life
V: moribund, unlikely to survive 24 h
VI: brain dead organ donor; E = emergency
ASA IV and V need a high-risk consent signed by the family

children.label: Cardiac risk indices
children: Goldman: S3 or raised JVP 11, MI within 6 months 10, non-sinus rhythm 7, over 5 PVCs/min 7
Goldman: age over 70 5, emergency 4, poor health 3, major thoracic/abdominal/aortic surgery 3, aortic stenosis 3
Over 25 points: life-saving procedures only
RCRI factors: IHD, CHF, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated DM, creatinine over 2.0, high-risk surgery
RCRI event rate: 0 factors 0.5%, 1 factor 1.3%, 2 factors 3.6%, 3 or more 9.1%

children.label: Hypertension
children: Mild (140-159/90-99): no need to delay surgery
Moderate (160-179/100-109): review treatment, monitor closely
Severe (over 180/109): postpone elective surgery

children.label: Premedication
children: Reduce anxiety and pain, promote amnesia, reduce secretions
Reduce gastric volume and pH to avoid Mendelson's syndrome (aspiration pneumonitis)
Reduce PONV and vagal reflexes, enhance hypnosis, prevent endocarditis
H2 blocker or PPI hours before, oral sodium citrate 15-30 min before induction

children.label: High-risk groups
children: Elderly: fragile CVS, small doses cause hypotension, hypothermia risk
Emergency surgery in the elderly: 4 to 20 times higher mortality
Paediatrics: high risk, hypothermia risk

children.label: Overview
children: Observation: skin color, chest movement during ventilation
Equipment monitoring
Qualified anesthesia personnel present throughout
HR and BP measured every 5 min, drugs and fluids charted
Oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and temperature continually evaluated

children.label: Normal values under anesthesia
children: SBP 85-160, DBP 50-95 mmHg
SpO2 95-100%, ETCO2 33-45 mmHg
Temperature 36-37.5 °C
Urine output 0.5 ml/kg/min or more (as written in the lecture)
CVP 1-10 mmHg, MAP 80-120 mmHg
MAP = DBP + 1/3 (SBP - DBP)

children.label: Depth of anesthesia
children: BIS 40-60: recommended for general anesthesia
BIS below 40: deep; above 60: may be conscious; 60-90 sedation; 100 awake
Inadequate: grimacing, movement; if paralyzed, hypertension, tachycardia, tearing, sweating
Excessive: bradycardia, hypotension, cardiac depression
BIS may reduce intraoperative awareness

children.label: ECG
children: 3 leads usually (lead II), 5 leads for complicated patients
5-lead system adds V5 and limb leads
ST depression = ischemia, elevation = infarction
Over 85% of ischemic events seen in leads II and V5
P wave in lead II helps identify sinus rhythm

children.label: Pulse oximetry
children: Measures Hb saturation (normal above 90%, usually 97-98%)
Red and infrared light absorption difference between oxyHb and deoxyHb
CO poisoning gives falsely high reading
Inaccurate with poor perfusion, vasoconstriction, movement, dysrhythmia, cautery interference, methylene blue

children.label: Blood pressure
children: Palpation (SBP only), Korotkoff auscultation, automated non-invasive, invasive arterial
Automated cuff measures every ~5 min and may stop reading in sudden severe hypotension
Invasive indications: rapid BP changes, frequent sampling, major surgery, vasoactive drugs
Also burns, morbid obesity, severe metabolic abnormality, major trauma
Radial artery is the most common site; femoral, brachial, dorsalis pedis alternatives

children.label: Central venous pressure
children: Line in internal jugular, subclavian or femoral vein reaching SVC or IVC
Reflects RA and RV pressure, intravascular volume, RV preload
Measure at end-expiration, trends more useful than single values
Not needed for minor surgery
Right internal jugular: predictable landmarks, straight course, 90-99% success
Complications: infection, bleeding, air embolism, pneumothorax, carotid puncture, arrhythmia
Chest X-ray after upper-body insertion; ultrasound guidance helps

children.label: Capnography and ETCO2
children: Capnometry = number, capnogram = waveform, capnography = continuous monitoring
Under GA keep ETCO2 about 32-35, not below 30 (cerebral vasoconstriction)
PaCO2 minus ETCO2 about 5 mmHg
Best method to confirm intubation and extubation
Also adequacy of ventilation, PE, partial obstruction, bronchospasm, resuscitation outcome
Increased: hyperthermia, sepsis, thyroid storm, MH, hypoventilation, rebreathing, laparoscopy
Decreased: hypothermia, hyperventilation, hypoperfusion, embolism
Waveform: phase I dead space, II upstroke, III alveolar plateau, IV downstroke

children.label: Cyanosis
children: Defined as 5 g/dL deoxygenated hemoglobin
Normal Hb 15: SaO2 66%, PaO2 35 mmHg
Anemic Hb 10: SaO2 50%, PaO2 27 mmHg
In anemia, cyanosis appears at a lower oxygen tension

children.label: Oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve
children: Sigmoid curve of PaO2 against saturation
Below PaO2 60 (SpO2 90%) saturation falls rapidly; lowest acceptable SpO2 is 90%
Left shift: alkalosis, low 2,3-DPG, hypothermia, low CO2, fetal Hb, COHb, methemoglobin; higher affinity
Right shift: acidosis, high CO2, hyperthermia, high 2,3-DPG, altitude, sickle cell, inhalational agents; lower affinity
Right shift releases O2 to tissues more easily
O2 content = binding capacity x saturation + dissolved O2

children.label: Temperature and urine output
children: Keep theatre at 22 °C or higher
Heat loss under anesthesia 0.5-1 °C per hour; below 34 °C significant morbidity
High risk: elderly, burns, neonates, spinal cord injury
Hyperthermia causes: MH, pyrogens, overwarming, thyrotoxicosis, pheochromocytoma
Sites: tympanic, esophagus, rectum, nasopharynx
Foley catheter in major surgery; below 0.5 ml/kg/min is oliguria
Choose monitors by surgery size (no CVP, arterial line or BIS for appendectomy)

children.label: Basics
children: Anesthesia: reversible loss of consciousness and analgesia, with or without muscle relaxation (lecturer adds amnesia)
Phases: induction (mainly IV), maintenance (mainly inhalational), recovery
Gas (N2O in cylinders) or liquid via temperature-compensated vaporizer
Pathway: machine, vapor-oxygen mixture, lungs, blood, brain
Concentration example: 2 L O2 + 4 L N2O gives N2O 66%

children.label: MAC
children: Alveolar concentration at 1 atm preventing movement in 50% of patients at incision
Lower MAC means more potent; 1.2-1.3 MAC blocks movement in 95%
MAC: N2O 105%, enflurane 1.68%, isoflurane 1.16%, sevoflurane 2%, desflurane 6%, halothane 0.75%
Potency: halothane > isoflurane > enflurane > sevoflurane > desflurane > N2O
Higher MAC: hyperthermia, chronic alcohol use, acute amphetamines, hyperthyroidism
Lower MAC: old age, hypothermia, opioids, acute alcohol, pregnancy, hypothyroidism, clonidine
No effect: gender, duration of anesthesia, CO2 tension, hypertension, hyperkalemia

children.label: Uptake
children: To alveoli: higher delivered concentration, gas flow, minute ventilation
To brain: blood flow to brain, brain solubility, arteriovenous concentration difference
Agent moves along a partial pressure gradient and must be lipid soluble

children.label: Nitrous oxide
children: Only inhalational agent with analgesia; weak anesthetic used as adjuvant
Non-flammable, odorless, not metabolized, rapid diffusion
Diffusion hypoxia at end of surgery: give supplemental O2
Expands closed gas spaces: avoid in pneumothorax, bowel obstruction, middle ear surgery
Minimal CVS depression
Teratogenic with prolonged occupational exposure of staff; use scavenging
Second gas effect: fast N2O uptake speeds rise of a companion gas

children.label: Halothane
children: Most potent (MAC 0.75%), blood/gas coefficient 2.5, smooth induction
Bronchodilator, muscle relaxant, uterine relaxant
Arrhythmias: sensitizes myocardium to catecholamines
Poor analgesia, postoperative shivering, severe PONV
Hepatotoxicity: mild type 1 (25-30%), fulminant immune type 2 (1 in 6,000-35,000, mortality 30-80%)
Avoid repeat exposure within 3 months; ask about jaundice or fever after earlier use
Still used in Jordan because it is cheap

children.label: Enflurane and isoflurane
children: Enflurane: potent CV depressant, lowers seizure threshold (avoid in epilepsy), renal risk
Isoflurane: pungent, causes cough and breath-holding, used for maintenance not induction
Isoflurane: rapid recovery, cardiovascular stability, little hepatic or renal toxicity
Isoflurane: coronary vasodilation, coronary steal syndrome

children.label: Coronary steal syndrome
children: Vasodilator diverts blood from ischemic to normal myocardium
Narrowed arteries are already maximally dilated
Creates more ischemia in the diseased zone

children.label: Sevoflurane and desflurane
children: Sevoflurane: MAC 2%, sweet non-irritant, fastest induction, agent of choice for inhalational induction
Sevoflurane: compound A with soda lime (toxic to brain, liver, kidney), about 5% metabolized
Sevoflurane: postoperative agitation in children, does not sensitize myocardium much
Desflurane: MAC 6%, low potency, electrically heated vaporizer
Desflurane: poor induction agent, rapid recovery

children.label: Malignant hyperthermia
children: Triggers: all volatile agents (not N2O) and succinylcholine
Autosomal dominant, RYR1 mutation causes excess Ca2+ release from sarcoplasmic reticulum
Signs: muscle rigidity, tachycardia, rising CO2 production, fever (about 1 °C per 5 min)
Management: 100% O2, stop volatile agent
Cool the body and give fluids
IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg bolus then infusion over 72 h
Treat acidosis and hyperkalemia

children.label: Ideal IV agent
children: Rapid onset: lipid soluble and mostly un-ionized at blood pH
Rapid recovery through redistribution
Analgesia at sub-anesthetic doses
Minimal CVS and respiratory depression
No nausea, excitation, emergence phenomena or histamine release
No pain on injection, no venous sequelae, water soluble
Does not stimulate porphyria

children.label: Classification
children: Barbiturate: thiopental
Non-barbiturate: propofol, ketamine, etomidate
Adjuvants: benzodiazepines (midazolam, diazepam)

children.label: Thiopental
children: Ultra-short barbiturate, 3-5 mg/kg gives sleep in 30-60 s
Usual induction 3-6 mg/kg; very small doses in shock or frail elderly
Short action from redistribution to muscle and fat
Enhances GABA; lowers ICP and intraocular pressure
Myocardial depression, hypotension, apnea, laryngospasm
Contraindications: airway obstruction, porphyria, hypersensitivity
Caution: CVS, hepatic and renal disease
Intra-arterial injection: dilute with saline, heparinize, brachial plexus block

children.label: Propofol
children: Alkylphenol; 1% emulsion (soybean oil, glycerol, egg phosphatide)
Induction 2.5-3 mg/kg (1.5-2 premedicated, 1 or less elderly)
TIVA 50-150 mcg/kg/min; sedation 25-75 mcg/kg/min
No histamine release, no MH trigger, low PONV, antiemetic and anticonvulsant
Lowers cerebral blood flow and ICP
Hypotension more than thiopental and impaired baroreflex; profound respiratory depression
Pain on injection: add lidocaine or use a larger vein
Contraindications (slide): egg allergy, cannot maintain airway, fixed cardiac output, shock

children.label: Ketamine
children: Dissociative agent related to PCP, acts on NMDA receptors
IV 1-2 mg/kg, IM 5-10 mg/kg
Raises BP, heart rate, cardiac output, ICP and intraocular pressure
Bronchodilator, preserves airway reflexes, increases secretions
Unpleasant dreams, hallucinations, delirium
Uses: asthmatics, CV collapse needing emergency surgery, induction
Contraindications: psychosis, cerebrovascular disease, hypertension hazardous, raised ICP

children.label: Etomidate
children: Acts on GABA receptors, induction 0.2-0.3 mg/kg
Hemodynamically neutral, no analgesia
Adverse: nausea and vomiting, injection pain, myoclonus
Transient adrenal insufficiency: caution with chronic steroids

children.label: Benzodiazepines
children: Amnesia, anticonvulsant, minimal cardiorespiratory depression
Facilitate GABA; metabolized by liver conjugation
Midazolam: 2-3x more potent, faster onset, more amnesia, half-life 1-4 h
Diazepam: longer acting (21-37 h), more post-op sedation, more injection pain
Flumazenil: competitive antagonist, 0.2 mg over 15 s then 0.1 mg/min up to 2 mg
Flumazenil half-life about 1 h, so sedation may recur

children.label: Opioids
children: Opium alkaloids: morphine (strongest), codeine
Mu: analgesia, respiratory depression, euphoria, dependence
Kappa: analgesia, sedation, miosis; sigma: dysphoria
Fentanyl: opioid most used for induction, 100x morphine potency, about 30 min
Morphine: long analgesia, give under 5 mg/min (histamine release)
Effects: slow deep breathing, bradycardia, low SVR, constipation, biliary colic, urinary retention, chest wall rigidity
Naloxone reverses (onset 1-2 min, lasts 30-60 min); high doses cause abrupt pain, hypertension, pulmonary edema, arrest

children.label: Structure and classification
children: Aromatic ring (lipophilic), intermediate chain, tertiary amine (hydrophilic)
Esters: cocaine, procaine, chloroprocaine
Amides (two i's): lidocaine, prilocaine, bupivacaine, etidocaine, mepivacaine
Esters: unstable, hydrolyzed by plasma cholinesterase, PABA allergy
Amides: stable, slowly metabolized by liver, longer acting, allergy extremely rare

children.label: Mechanism
children: Block Na+ channels, inhibiting the action potential in unmyelinated fibres
Only the unionized base crosses the membrane
Acidic tissue (abscess, inflammation): less free base, weak or failed block
Adding sodium bicarbonate raises pH and gives more base

children.label: Preparations
children: Acidic solutions (pH 4-5.5), hydrochloride salts
May contain vasoconstrictor, reducing agent (metabisulphite), preservative
1% = 10 mg/mL (mg/mL = % x 10)

children.label: Vasoconstrictors
children: Adrenaline 1:80,000 to 1:300,000 is most common
Slow absorption, lower toxicity, longer duration, less bleeding
Maximum dose: lidocaine 3 mg/kg plain, 7 with adrenaline
Maximum dose: prilocaine 6 plain, 9 with adrenaline; bupivacaine 2 either way
Never use around end-arteries (fingers, penis) or in IVRA
Relative: severe hypertension, GA with halothane

children.label: Clinical uses
children: Topical: lidocaine gel, EMLA (lidocaine 2.5% + prilocaine 2.5%)
Infiltration for minor surgery
Peripheral nerve blocks (nerve stimulator or ultrasound)
Intravenous regional anesthesia, spinal, epidural
Always aspirate before injecting

children.label: IVRA (Bier's block)
children: Upper limb surgery under 1 h
Two cannulae: one in the affected limb, one in the other limb for resuscitation
Exsanguinate with Esmarch band, inflate proximal cuff above systolic pressure
Inject lidocaine or prilocaine after removing the band
Cuff stays inflated at least 20 min, then deflate gradually
Never bupivacaine or etidocaine: cardiotoxic

children.label: Individual agents
children: Lidocaine: first amide, local anesthetic and antiarrhythmic, blocks fast Na+ channels
Bupivacaine: long duration, most cardiotoxic, not given IV, used spinal or epidural
Benzocaine: topical only, causes methemoglobinemia

children.label: Toxicity
children: Causes: accidental IV injection, rapid absorption from vascular sites, overdose
CNS first: dizziness, tinnitus, circumoral numbness, blurred vision, metallic taste
Severe: convulsions, coma, respiratory arrest
CVS: bradycardia and hypotension without adrenaline; myocardial depression leads to collapse
Prevent: secure IV access and have resuscitation equipment ready
Treat: stop injection, call help, ABC, O2, ventilate, fluids, ephedrine, atropine
Convulsions: diazepam 0.2-0.4 mg/kg or thiopentone 1-4 mg/kg

children.label: Antidotes
children: Bupivacaine: 20% lipid emulsion IV (Intralipid, not a true antidote)
Benzocaine methemoglobinemia: low-dose methylene blue
Lidocaine: diphenhydramine (as written on the slide)

children.label: Classification
children: Regional anesthesia: neuraxial block (spinal, epidural/caudal) and peripheral nerve block
Spinal: injection into the CSF (subarachnoid space)
Epidural: injection into the epidural space
Adults: inject L3-L4, L4-L5 or L5-S1 (cord ends L1-L2)
Children: inject L4-L5 or L5-S1 (cord ends L2-L3)
Spinal gives anesthesia below the umbilicus (T10)

children.label: Advantages of spinal
children: Low cost and high patient satisfaction
Few respiratory effects, airway preserved, less aspiration risk
Cesarean: less drug transfer to the baby
Diabetics stay awake and notice hypoglycemia
Excellent muscle relaxation, less blood loss
Better gut blood flow, faster return of gut function
Fewer DVT and PE, avoids GA complications

children.label: Indications
children: Operations below the umbilicus: hernia, gynecologic, urologic, cesarean, lower limb orthopedics
Perineum and genitalia surgery
Elderly and chronic systemic disease
Surgery must last about 2-3 hours or less

children.label: Contraindications
children: Absolute: patient refusal, uncooperative patient, coagulopathy or anticoagulants
Absolute: infection at site, septicemia, severe aortic or mitral stenosis
Absolute: hypovolemia, raised ICP
Relative: anatomical deformity, neurological disease, previous spinal surgery
Relative: inadequate resuscitation equipment

children.label: Drugs and baricity
children: Hyperbaric solutions settle downward and are most predictable
Hypobaric rise; isobaric stay near the injection site
Bupivacaine 0.5% hyperbaric: best, lasts 2-3 h
Lidocaine 5% hyperbaric: lasts 45-90 min
Do not use multi-dose lidocaine vials intrathecally (preservatives)

children.label: Factors affecting spread
children: Baricity of the solution and position of the patient
Level and speed of injection
Obesity and pregnancy: reduce the dose

children.label: Technique
children: Consent, normotensive patient, aseptic technique
Sitting or lateral position with spine flexed
Line between iliac crests marks L4
Wheal of local anesthetic first
Needle passes skin, supraspinous, interspinous, ligamentum flavum (first pop), dura (second pop)
CSF confirms entry; inject slowly
Block order: autonomic, sensory, motor; recovery in reverse

children.label: Complications of spinal
children: Hypotension (most common): preload fluids, raise legs, ephedrine, atropine for bradycardia
Post-dural puncture headache (2nd most common): postural, onset 12-24 h
Prevent PDPH with small pencil-point needle
PDPH treatment: bed rest, paracetamol, hydration, caffeine, epidural blood patch last
Urinary retention
Rare: meningitis, arachnoiditis, epidural abscess, hematoma, paralysis

children.label: Epidural anesthesia
children: Space between dura mater and ligamentum flavum; dura not punctured
Tuohy needle (about 18 G) with loss of resistance technique
Catheter allows continuous infusion for labor and postoperative pain
Bupivacaine 0.5% or lidocaine 2%
Same indications and complications as spinal except post-dural puncture headache
Accidental dural puncture with a large needle causes severe headache

children.label: Spinal vs epidural
children: Spinal: below L1/L2, subarachnoid, single shot, CSF confirms
Epidural: any level, no dural puncture, continuous, loss of resistance confirms
Dose: spinal 2.5-3.5 mL bupivacaine 0.5% heavy; epidural 15-20 mL 0.5%
Onset: spinal 2-5 min; epidural 15-20 min
Spinal: denser block, rapid hypotension; epidural: less dense, slow hypotension

children.label: Overview
children: Three phases: induction, maintenance, recovery
IV induction is used in most cases
Airway options: face mask, laryngeal mask, tracheal tube

children.label: Inhalational induction
children: Indications: young children, upper airway obstruction (epiglottitis)
Indications: lower airway foreign body, bronchopleural fistula or empyema, no accessible veins
IV agents cause apnea; inhalational agents preserve breathing
Start with 70% N2O in O2, deepen with volatile agent (halothane 1-3%)
Difficulties: slow induction, bronchospasm, laryngospasm, hiccups, pollution

children.label: Maintenance
children: Inhalational agents: sevoflurane, isoflurane, halothane 1-2 MAC with 70% N2O
IV agents and IV opioids (fentanyl, alfentanil, remifentanil)
TIVA: propofol plus opioid
Choice depends on surgery, premedication analgesia and patient response
Spontaneous ventilation suits superficial, minor procedures

children.label: Complications during maintenance
children: Airway obstruction: positioning and equipment
Laryngeal spasm: stop stimulation, deepen anesthesia, 100% O2, suxamethonium if severe
Bronchospasm: deepen anesthesia, IV or endotracheal lidocaine 1-2 mg/kg, bronchodilators
Malignant hyperthermia: volatile agents and suxamethonium trigger
Raised ICP worsened by CO2 retention
Atmospheric pollution: scavenging apparatus

children.label: Face mask
children: Correct fit for a gas-tight seal (sizes 00-6)
Hold the mandible forward, hold rather than press
Obstruction signs: soft-tissue indrawing, noisy breathing, inspiratory stridor
Guedel oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway helps
Reach proper depth before inserting an airway to avoid coughing or laryngospasm

children.label: Laryngeal mask airway
children: Insertion: head extended, mouth open, pre-deflated mask swept into laryngopharynx, inflate cuff, confirm, secure
Indications: clear airway without mask, spontaneous ventilation, difficult intubation
Contraindications: full stomach, regurgitation risk, impeded surgical access
Also thoracic surgery, prone position, pregnancy over 12 weeks

children.label: Tracheal intubation
children: Prepare equipment, experienced assistant, laryngoscope, tube patency
Indications: clear airway, airway hard to control (prone, sitting, lateral), head and neck surgery
Indications: protect from aspiration, suction, chest/abdomen/cranium surgery, respiratory failure, positive-pressure ventilation
Under GA with or without relaxant, or awake with topical spray and superior laryngeal nerve block
Relaxant: suxamethonium 1-1.5 mg/kg
Inhalational technique: halothane up to 4%, diaphragmatic breathing confirms depth

children.label: Tube details
children: Paediatric size = age/4 + 4
Adult: female 7-7.5, male 7.5-8.5
Cuff: fixation, prevents aspiration, prevents gas leak
Confirm: laryngoscope view, chest movement, vapour in tube, auscultation, capnography, X-ray
Esophageal intubation: fixed chest and distended abdomen

children.label: Complications of intubation
children: Early: lip and teeth trauma, jaw dislocation, vocal cord damage, epistaxis
Early: obstruction or kinking, bronchial intubation, arrhythmias and hypertension
Late: tracheal stenosis, mucosal damage, vocal cord ulceration, hoarseness

children.label: Recovery and extubation
children: Stop inhalational agent; reverse atracurium with neostigmine plus atropine
Extubate when reflexes return and vital signs are normal
Lateral position if risk of regurgitation
100% O2 before extubation to avoid diffusion hypoxia
Preoxygenate, then suction the tube, extubate during inspiration
Complications: laryngospasm, regurgitation, hypertension and tachycardia, glottic edema
Recovery room: BP, RR, HR, temperature, SpO2, pain compared with preoperative vitals

children.label: Neuromuscular junction
children: Motor nerve ending, synaptic cleft (20-30 nm), folded muscle membrane, nicotinic receptors
Action potential, Ca2+ influx, ACh exocytosis, ACh binds receptor
Cation influx depolarizes the fiber, Na+ channels fire an action potential
Acetylcholinesterase breaks ACh into acetate and choline

children.label: Classification
children: Spasmolytics relieve spasm toward normal tone
Neuromuscular blockers paralyze muscle completely
Depolarizing: succinylcholine, agonist
Non-depolarizing: competitive antagonists (e.g. tubocurarine)
Ultra-short: succinylcholine; short: mivacurium
Intermediate: vecuronium, rocuronium, atracurium, cisatracurium; long: pancuronium

children.label: Role in surgery
children: Given with anesthetics at induction
Facilitate intra-abdominal and intrathoracic surgery and intubation
All respiratory muscles are paralyzed: ventilation must be available

children.label: Succinylcholine
children: Binds nicotinic receptors: depolarization, fasciculations, then desensitization and paralysis
Broken down by plasma pseudocholinesterase, not acetylcholinesterase
Intubating dose 1-2 mg/kg IV, peak within 60 s, lasts 5-10 min
No antagonist; prolonged in cholinesterase deficiency, liver disease, pregnancy
Indications: full stomach or emergency, cesarean, predicted difficult intubation, ECT, short procedures

children.label: Succinylcholine adverse effects
children: Raised intraocular and intracranial pressure
Myalgia, myoglobinuria, masseter spasm
Bradycardia, dysrhythmia, sinus arrest
Hyperkalemia: normal rise 0.5 mEq/L, up to 13 in high-risk patients
High risk: extensive burns, severe closed head injury, UMN lesion, muscular dystrophy, traumatic paralysis
Contraindications: cannot maintain airway, allergy, MH history, K+ 5.5 or more, myotonia

children.label: Non-depolarizing blockers
children: Compete with ACh at the same receptor; onset 3-4 min
Paralysis order: face and eyes, fingers and limbs, neck and trunk, intercostals, diaphragm last
Recovery in reverse order; given IV only
Prolonged by acidosis, hypothermia, age, low K+ or Ca2+, volatile agents
Reversed with neostigmine plus atropine

children.label: Individual drugs
children: Vecuronium: intermediate, no CVS effects
Rocuronium: onset under 1 min at 0.6 mg/kg, choice when succinylcholine is contraindicated
Cisatracurium: Hofmann degradation, no histamine release, ideal in renal or hepatic failure
Atracurium: releases histamine (avoid in asthmatics)
Pancuronium: long-acting, raises HR and BP, renal excretion

children.label: Anticholinergics
children: Atropine: muscarinic antagonist, crosses BBB, minimum 20 mcg/kg (less causes paradoxical bradycardia)
Atropine effects: tachycardia, mydriasis, dry mouth, bronchodilation, hyperthermia
Overdose: hot as a hare, mad as a hatter, red as a beet, dry as a bone
Atropine uses: block neostigmine effects, reduce secretions, organophosphate antidote
Avoid in closed-angle glaucoma and prostatic hyperplasia
Scopolamine: more CNS effect, amnesia, motion sickness
Glycopyrrolate: most commonly used, no CNS effect, less CV stimulation

children.label: Cholinesterase inhibitors
children: Prolong ACh life; reversible (neostigmine, physostigmine), irreversible (echothiophate)
Neostigmine: most commonly used, 2.5-5 mg IV to reverse non-depolarizing block
Side effects: bradycardia, miosis, salivation, bronchospasm, GI hypermotility
Give atropine with neostigmine in one syringe
Other uses: urinary retention after GA, myasthenia gravis
